title: Through the window (1 Samuel 19:11–17)
hookLine: Michal lets David down through a window to escape her father

cards: Night, and there are men outside the house. King Saul has sent them to watch David's door and kill him in the morning. Inside are David and his wife, Michal, Saul's own daughter.
A chapter earlier the text said plainly that Michal loved David. Now she tells him: if you don't save your life tonight, tomorrow you'll be killed. The front door is watched.
She has a house, a husband, a father who is the king, and maybe a few hours. What she does next happens at a window.

teach.b: The verse is short and fast: "So Michal let David down through the window; and he went, and fled, and escaped." Three verbs for David, like footsteps. Then Michal turns back into the room and buys him time.
She lays the household image the text calls teraphim in the bed, puts a pillow of goats' hair where his head would be, and covers it with a cloth. When Saul's messengers come, she says David is sick.
Saul sends them back: bring him to me in the bed, so I can kill him. They pull back the cover and find the image and the goats' hair.
Now Michal is the one facing her father. Why did you deceive me and let my enemy escape? She answers with a story: David said to her, let me go, why should I kill you?

teach.h: HE WENT, AND FLED, AND ESCAPED.
teach.b: It may not be true; the text doesn't say. It reads like a daughter shielding herself from a father who has already thrown a spear at David. So the window works two ways.
It's how David gets out, and it's where Michal stays behind. Her rescue costs her something, and the story lets her pay it alone.
One small echo: the heading of Psalm fifty-nine ties that psalm to this very night, when Saul sent men to watch the house. A prayer, by tradition, from inside the danger she helped him out of.

how: Jews read Michal's rescue of David in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets; Psalm 59, whose heading ties it to this night, is read in the book of Psalms.

practice: Danger doesn't always look like men at the door: a friend in a bad stretch, a coworker getting blamed, a kid being picked on.
Let one person come to mind, and look for the window, the one small opening you could give them: a call, a word to the right person, a ride. If you pray, you can hold that person by name.
